stemMd:
Having photographed the front of the Kvarn Glacier from the same ridge every August for eleven years, ______ that the ice had retreated by nearly four hundred meters.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

options.label: A
options.textMd: the photographs taken by glaciologist Ilse Brandt showed

options.label: C
options.textMd: it became clear to glaciologist Ilse Brandt

explanationMd:
A sentence that opens with an *-ing* phrase and then a comma makes a promise: the first noun after the comma is the one doing the action in the phrase. So ask who did the photographing. Only a person could have *photographed the front of the Kvarn Glacier ... every August*, so the subject of the main clause must be that person.

The only choice whose subject is Ilse Brandt herself is **glaciologist Ilse Brandt could show**.

The hardest trap is the possessive. In *glaciologist Ilse Brandt's photographs showed*, Brandt's name comes first, and it feels as if she is the subject; but *Brandt's* is only a modifier of the real subject, *photographs*, and photographs cannot photograph a glacier. The choice beginning *it became clear to* also names Brandt, but puts her inside a prepositional phrase and makes the empty pronoun *it* the subject.

Check by joining the phrase directly to the subject of each choice: "photographs, having photographed...", "it, having photographed...", "Brandt, having photographed...". Only the last makes sense.

distractorRationale.d: This is the possessive trap. The subject of the clause is 'photographs', with 'Brandt's' only describing them, so the sentence says the photographs photographed the glacier for eleven years, a dangling modifier.
distractorRationale.c: The subject here is the pronoun 'it', not Brandt, who appears only as the object of 'to'. The opening phrase is left describing 'it', so the modifier dangles even though the right person is named.
distractorRationale.a: The subject is 'the photographs', so the opening phrase says the photographs did the photographing. Naming Brandt in the phrase 'taken by' does not make her the subject.

accessibilityText: A sentence that opens with the phrase 'Having photographed the front of the Kvarn Glacier from the same ridge every August for eleven years,' followed by a blank and the words 'that the ice had retreated by nearly four hundred meters.' Choose how to complete the sentence from four choices: the photographs taken by glaciologist Ilse Brandt showed; glaciologist Ilse Brandt could show; it became clear to glaciologist Ilse Brandt; and glaciologist Ilse Brandt's photographs showed.

provenance.notes: Original item. The Kvarn Glacier and Ilse Brandt are invented; no source text was adapted.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The opening participial phrase 'Having photographed ...' needs as its subject the person who photographed. Only B makes Brandt the subject. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: The opening participial phrase 'Having photographed...' has to modify the person who photographed, so Brandt must be the subject. A and D make the photographs the subject, and C uses 'it'; all three are dangling modifiers.]

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: The introductory participial phrase must modify the subject of the main clause, and only a person can have done the photographing. Only 'glaciologist Ilse Brandt could show' makes Brandt the subject. The possessive 'Brandt's photographs', 'the photographs taken by', and the dummy 'it became clear to' all leave the modifier dangling while still naming Brandt. Every choice completes a grammatical main clause with 'that the ice had retreated...', so the item turns only on modifier placement. Re-solved from the stem alone: same answer. Unique. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
